output.answer_markdown:
## Klaviyo flow configuration

Build as a new **First-time Daypack post-purchase** flow. Trigger on a paid Shopify order containing SKU `DAY18`, with `Placed Order = 1 over all time`. Require valid marketing consent unless counsel confirms a message qualifies as transactional.

Randomly assign 10% of otherwise eligible buyers to a persistent holdout before the first email. Holdout customers receive none of these three messages but may continue receiving normal transactional notices and campaigns.

Before every send, exclude customers whose Daypack order is cancelled, fully refunded, returned, or has an active return request. Suppress the review and cross-sell for unresolved support cases. If support status is not available in Klaviyo, maintain an exclusion segment until an integration is available.

Use the carrier or delivery platform’s confirmed-delivery event—not an estimated order-age calculation—for Emails 2 and 3. Customers without confirmed delivery remain waiting and exit after 30 days without receiving either message. Keep Shopify’s normal order and shipping notifications active; this flow does not replace them.

Report treatment versus holdout using Shopify order data, not Klaviyo-attributed revenue. Do not interpret opens, clicks, or platform attribution as repeat-purchase lift.

actions.primary_metric: 60-day net product revenue per eligible first-time Daypack buyer, treatment versus persistent holdout, using Shopify revenue net of refunds
secondary_metrics: 60-day accessory net product revenue per eligible buyer
Daypack review submission rate among delivered, eligible recipients
eligibility: Shopify paid order contains SKU DAY18
Placed Order equals 1 over all time at flow entry
Order is not cancelled or fully refunded
suppression: Suppress all remaining messages when the Daypack is returned, refunded, cancelled, or has an active return request
Suppress Emails 2 and 3 while a support issue is unresolved
Suppress Email 3 if the customer has purchased both POUCH and BOTTLE since entering
Exclude internal, test, fraudulent, and chargeback profiles

emails.name: Daypack onboarding
emails.event: Shopify Fulfilled Order or shipment-created event for the DAY18 order
emails.subject: Three useful notes before your Daypack arrives
emails.body:
Hi {{ first_name|default:'there' }},

Your Daypack 18L is on its way. You can get the latest carrier update here:

[TRACK MY ORDER]

A few useful notes before it arrives:

• The padded laptop sleeve is designed for a 13-inch laptop. We have not verified fit for 15-inch models, so please don’t rely on the sleeve for one.
• The fabric is water-resistant, not waterproof. For sustained or heavy rain, give electronics and other sensitive items additional protection.
• The external pocket gives you a separate place for a bottle.

Our standard US delivery estimate is 4–7 business days, but the carrier tracking page is the best source for the latest timing. If something looks wrong, reply to this email and we’ll help.

Unused products may be returned within 30 days; return shipping is paid by the customer. Full details: [RETURNS POLICY]

— TrailFold

emails.name: Daypack review request
emails.event: Confirmed Delivered event matched to the DAY18 shipment
emails.subject: How is your Daypack working out?
emails.body:
Hi {{ first_name|default:'there' }},

You’ve had a little time with your Daypack 18L. Would you leave an honest review?

Your experience can help another commuter understand whether the size, laptop sleeve, and rain protection are right for them.

[REVIEW THE DAYPACK]

The link should open the Daypack review form directly. We welcome candid feedback—positive or negative.

If you need help or something isn’t right, reply here instead and our team will assist.

— TrailFold

emails.name: Optional accessory cross-sell
emails.event: Confirmed Delivered event matched to the DAY18 shipment
emails.subject: Two optional additions to your Daypack
emails.body:
Hi {{ first_name|default:'there' }},

If your Daypack already covers what you need, you’re all set.

If you want to add another practical item, TrailFold also offers:

Cable pouch — $20
[VIEW CABLE POUCH]

Steel bottle — $32
[VIEW STEEL BOTTLE]

There’s no discount or deadline attached—just two optional additions to consider for your weekday or weekend setup.

US shipping is free. The standard delivery estimate is 4–7 business days.

— TrailFold

task.title: Post-purchase retention flow
task.request: Create a practical post-purchase email flow for first-time Daypack buyers with three actual emails: useful onboarding, review request and optional accessory cross-sell. Include event/timing, eligibility, suppression, returns/refunds, delivery uncertainty and a small holdout measurement. Bags are durable goods, not replenishable subscriptions. input.reference_guidance:
[0a935c9bd0919223a8ba4c36] Sequence the Post-Purchase Flow Around Shipping, Usage, Loyalty, Reviews and Cross-Sell
Applies when: Mapping the full email sequence and delays of a post-purchase flow for a physical product.
- Email 1 (~30 min): thank-you and buyer's remorse reduction (see related card).
- Email 2 (~2 days): build excitement for delivery by giving product usage instructions. This future-paces the customer using the product, reduces buyer's remorse, and pre-empts support questions. If you sell multiple product types, use product-based splits to tailor this email to the item bought.
- Email 3 (~10 days): introduce your loyalty program. The source argues this is the moment the customer is happy having received and tried the product, making it a natural point to enroll them and move a first-time buyer toward repeating. Note: the delay depends on your shipping times — the source sets it after expected delivery.
- Email 4 (~+3 days): ask for a review, since by now the customer has enough usage to have formed an opinion. Offer a discount code as a thank-you for reviewing — the source notes it's optional but useful because even non-reviewers get a code and may rebuy.
- Email 5 & 6 (~7 days later, then +1 day): cross-sell with a discount and a 48-hour deadline, followed by a plain-text 24-hour deadline email from the founder. The source says founder plain-text emails 'work so well.'
- The delay to delivery and the review ask depend on your product type and shipping times; adjust accordingly. If you sell consumables, the source notes you can add a 'replacement reminder' (e.g., a 30-day product prompting at day ~25).
Condition: Delays are the presenter's defaults and depend on shipping and product type — validate against your own data.
Condition: The source flags review flows may be better as a separate flow when using a dedicated review platform (e.g., Judge.me) with its own triggers; otherwise you can host the ask inside the post-purchase flow.

[55898f20e16116a726da3dca] Design Post-Purchase Flows Around First-Time vs. Returning Customers
Applies when: Planning the post-purchase flow that fires after an order, especially to improve first-purchase experience and repeat purchase.
- Trigger on placed order; add brand-specific filters (e.g., exclude subscription or B2B customers from the standard post-purchase content, or route them to a different flow).
- Do not schedule sends at a fixed time of day (e.g., 9 a.m.) — instead keep relative timing like '1 day after' so emails land when that buyer is typically active.
- For first-time buyers: thank them, then deliver education/resources and use cases so they get full value — a poor first experience makes a return purchase unlikely.
- Include a proactive plain-text customer-service check-in email ('how's it going, let us know if you need help'), which most brands skip and which requires no staff time once automated.
- Then move them toward a next purchase via subscription, loyalty, or other programs.
- Set a conditional split on 'placed order equals 1 over all time' to separate first-timers from returning customers, who instead get loyalty appreciation and personalized cross-sells.
Condition: The source notes post-purchase flows are highly brand-specific, so filters and content must be set per brand rather than copied.
Condition: The anti-9 a.m. opinion assumes buyer activity patterns match purchase time; it is a stated rationale, not a tested benchmark.

[586799a976b3fdfb456a34ce] Time post-purchase and replenishment SMS to the buy cycle
Applies when: Building the post-purchase and replenishment SMS flow for your store.
- Send SMS 1 around day 10–14 after order delivery, while the buyer is in the honeymoon phase: ask if they're enjoying the product and suggest cross-sell/upsell or a repeat purchase.
- For consumable/replenishment products, add SMS 2 timed to when the product runs out. Calculate it: e.g., Athletic Greens — 30-day supply plus 7-day delivery → send on ~day 35, 'are you running low? reorder.'
- Hold offers initially; the source recommends not adding discounts to these early post-purchase messages until later.
- Don't over-send: remember buyers also receive your campaign blasts, so two well-timed post-purchase messages are usually enough.
- Consider keeping all win-back-style post-purchase messages in one flow triggered on order placement.
Condition: The source says this flow varies so much brand-to-brand that no single verified template applies; the athletic-greens math is an illustration.
Condition: Replenishment timing depends on your own product consumption and delivery cycle.

[cf03cf0f0e81168879f6a1dd] Capture reviews with a specific, low-friction post-purchase ask
Applies when: Building product-page social proof, improving marketplace review volume, or creating a referral and review flow after delivery or successful first use.
- Choose the moment when the customer has likely experienced value: after delivery confirmation for a giftable product, after first successful use for a tool, or after a replenishment purchase for a consumable.
- Ask for one action only, such as rating the product or leaving a review, and explain how that helps future shoppers choose with confidence.
- Make the request channel-specific. Link directly to the relevant review location and provide concise device instructions only after verifying the current interface.
- Use automation to trigger the ask by delivery date, estimated usage time, or a positive customer-service interaction rather than sending it immediately after checkout.
- Segment requests where practical: do not ask customers with unresolved support issues for a review; first resolve the issue.
- Encourage organic sharing by making the useful asset easy to pass along, such as a product-use guide or gift recommendation, without implying that a review requires compensation.
Condition: Review-platform interfaces and policies change; verify both the current UI and incentive rules before publishing instructions.
Condition: Do not pressure customers for only positive reviews or suppress legitimate negative feedback.

[6d6e184eb84866186d1e8f11] Convert shipping and delivery emails into education touchpoints
Applies when: Designing the order-confirmation, shipping, and delivery-notification sequence for any product that requires setup or a routine.
- Assume the period between purchase and delivery creates anticipation plus subconscious anxiety (post-purchase dissonance) — silence breeds it.
- For each post-purchase email, add product-specific education instead of only a tracking link: how to prepare before the product arrives, what physical sensations to expect on first use, and a realistic timeline to visible results.
- Use the messages to reinforce the correctness of the buying decision, which is the stated purpose of combating dissonance.
- Sequence them so the last message before delivery sets up the unboxing moment as the peak.
- Keep expectations accurate here — an inflated timeline claim becomes negative disconfirmation later.
Condition: The source presents this as a design principle for considered or routine-based products (its example is a personalized skincare regimen); for commodity reorders, the education payload may be thin.
Condition: Don't overload transactional emails with content that delays the tracking information customers actually open the message for.
Condition: Keep transactional messages focused on the order and necessary usage information; place promotional cross-sells in appropriately permitted marketing messages.

[1cdf5f4a3630ac18b9ae9cf8] Request visual reviews with compliant incentives
Applies when: Developing a post-purchase review collection flow to create more visual proof for product pages and paid-traffic landing pages.
- Ask customers after delivery or sufficient product-use time for a genuine review, specifically inviting photos or video when appropriate.
- Offer a modest incentive such as a future-order gift card only after checking the applicable advertising, consumer-protection, review-platform, and disclosure rules.
- Make clear that the incentive is for providing an honest review, not for giving a positive review.
- Store permissioned visual submissions in a searchable proof library organized by product, customer use case, outcome, and objection.
- Feature the most relevant submissions on the pages where their evidence supports a specific claim.
Condition: Rules differ by jurisdiction and review platform. Verify current requirements, including whether incentivized-review disclosure is required.
Condition: Never purchase fabricated, misleading, or selectively conditional positive reviews.

[d17748ab5f3a65537320cb01] Build a Three-Step Automated Post-Purchase Communication Flow
Applies when: Designing or auditing the transactional email/SMS flow between checkout and delivery for an ecommerce store.
- Send step 1, order confirmation, with a clear delivery estimate — not just a receipt. Include a link to your branded tracking page, a note on what happens next ('You'll receive a shipping confirmation within 24 hours') and a small piece of value such as a care guide, styling tip or founder note.
- Send step 2, shipping confirmation, with a working tracking link.
- Send step 3, out-for-delivery notification, with a delivery window.
- Make every step automatic so the customer never has to log in or search for status. The source states this three-step flow can eliminate up to 80% of WISMO tickets.
- Count your proactive touchpoints between order and delivery; if you send fewer than three automated updates, the source says you are leaving WISMO tickets and churn on the table.
- Use specific, urgency-revealing wording in confirmations (words like 'today', 'update', 'delivery') per Shopify's guidance cited in the source.
Condition: The up-to-80% WISMO reduction figure is a cited operational claim, not a guaranteed outcome; measure your own ticket volume before and after.

[31dde167599fd66b0eadeb26] The six baseline flows to build first, in order
Applies when: You are deciding which automated email flows to build or fix next, and whether to invest in advanced segmentation or upsell logic.
- Welcome flow: 8 emails for new subscribers.
- Site abandon flow: 1 email for someone who visited the site and left without deeper action.
- Browse abandon flow: 5 emails for someone who viewed a product and left.
- Cart abandon flow: 6-8 emails for someone who added to cart and left.
- Checkout abandon flow: 6-8 emails for someone who started checkout and left.
- Post-purchase flow: sequence after a purchase.
- Win-back flow: for customers who purchased months ago and have gone quiet.
- Audit your existing flows against these basics before adding advanced cross-sell, upsell or split tests — the source describes a case where a brand wanted advanced automations while the welcome flow was a single email and cart abandonment was not set up correctly.
Condition: Email counts per flow are the source's recommended structure; your optimal counts depend on catalog, price point and purchase frequency.
Condition: The described revenue improvement for one brand (roughly $45k to $133k in a month after fixing basics) is a case example, not a promised result.

[5956a124a134fee12227f6f0] Post-purchase email content: 6-email sequence
Applies when: Writing the emails in your post-purchase flow after a customer's first order.
- Email 1 (10 minutes): plain-text thank-you from the founder. Confirm order progress, offer support, tell them what to expect. For first-time buyers make it a memorable first impression; for returning customers express gratitude for loyalty. Include a link back to your site (source says even just a site link gets a strong post-purchase place-order rate) and optionally recommend a specific product to cross-sell — the biggest repeat-purchase window is the first 30 days.
- Email 2 (2 days): 'your order is on its way'. Build excitement, reinforce the value of the purchase, and include recommendations — static blocks or the Klaviyo product feed. Examples: refills/cookbook/candle/kit for a spice brand; 'complete your stack' bundles pairing isolate with creatine or collagen for a nutrition brand; 'explore more' sabers plus a mystery saber (curiosity works).
- Email 3: how-to email, split by product or product category so it's actually relevant to what they bought. Provide clear actionable tips, links to FAQs/manuals/videos, and reassurance they made a good choice. This reduces returns and improves experience.
- Email 4 (optional): social media follow push — the more channels you hold a customer on, the better for repeat purchase.
- Email 5 (optional): loyalty program push. Make the benefit immediately clear (points, discounts, rewards for shopping/reviewing/referring) — people only join for a clear benefit.
- Email 6: post-delivery plain-text check-in from the founder — 'how did everything go?' The source says this is one of the highest-revenue emails because it shows genuine care and can invite the next purchase.
Condition: Source claims retained customers are 9x more likely to convert and repeat customers spend 67% more than new customers; it does not provide the study for either, so treat as attributed statistics, not your expected results.
Condition: Source claims 95% of customers receiving proactive post-purchase communication are less likely to return — also unaudited data, use as directional.
Condition: The 'most returning customers buy within 30 days' statement is from one client screenshot, not a universal benchmark.
Condition: Auto-applied source framing: how-to email 3 only makes sense if you have technical products; simple care instructions may be enough for apparel.

[fd106fda6cf6c3e0b770c35a] Set Up Automated Review Request Emails (Delays, Templates, Branding)
Applies when: Building a post-purchase review collection flow to generate PDP social proof on a Shopify store.
- In Judge.me settings, set up the review request emails BEFORE scheduling any bulk requests to past customers.
- Configure delays under 'manage email review request': the default is 14 days for domestic orders and 5 for others. Adjust based on your niche — if products take time to try, increase the delay; if instant-use, lower it. You can set different delays for international and point-of-sale orders.
- Use 'schedule requests for previous Shopify orders' to bulk-request reviews from existing customers; use 'send manual request' for one-offs.
- Edit the review request and reminder templates: change the trigger (button vs. stars), language, subject line, and email title.
- Apply template styling globally (store logo, fonts, brand colors, alignment) via edit template styling — these apply to all emails.
- If you want customers to review without leaving the email, create a custom template from scratch, drag in the 'classic form' block, add the product image and product title (via email variables), and toggle the custom template on / default off.
- Set review publishing/moderation rules so you can approve reviews before they go live if you want full control.
Condition: Free plan may limit features; the presenter recommends the paid plan but acknowledges the free option exists.
Condition: Third-party review app UI and defaults change over time — verify current settings.

[1911a725b0874dacccec914f] Build a six-email post-purchase flow with timed emotional beats
Applies when: Setting up or rebuilding the post-purchase email flow for your store (replenishment/retention), especially if you currently only send an order confirmation and shipping notice.
- Set the trigger to 'order placed' with no filter so every buyer enters.
- Email 1 at 0 minutes: a plain, text-based thank-you from the founder. Split by purchase count (1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th+) and change the wording slightly each time (e.g., 'you're almost a VIP' for repeat buyers). Include four things: sincere thanks, mission reminder, support offer, and a P.S. inviting an add-on to the order.
- Email 2 at ~24 hours: 'want to add more.' Send a general cross-sell of best sellers or split by product/category for curated recommendations tied to what they bought.
- Email 3 at ~3 days: a 'get excited, your order is being handled' message. You don't need a delivery trigger — estimate timing and link products at the bottom.
- Email 4 at ~6 days: 'how to get the most out of your product.' Split by what they ordered and give usage tips; add a recommended-product section to pair complementary items. This also reduces returns from misuse.
- Email 5 at ~7 days: ask them to follow one social platform (pick a single one, not several).
- Email 6 at ~1-2 weeks: a founder check-in asking how the order went, offering support, and optionally a review or repurchase prompt.
- After launch, analyze numbers and add or remove emails over time — this is a starting point, not a fixed template.
Condition: Timing past the first day is estimated, not triggered by real delivery data.
Condition: The presenter's claimed $48,000 in 30 days is a single case example, not an expected result.
Condition: Higher-AOV products may see more buyer's remorse, so the reassurance emails matter more.

[bd18309bf03ec0ce58f5f4cd] Run Post-Checkout Upsells to Increase Basket Value
Applies when: Adding an upsell/cross-sell mechanic to the checkout completion or thank-you page without disrupting the purchase.
- Place the offer immediately after checkout, on the thank-you page, or via email — the source frames this as an ecommerce-specific retention tool.
- Choose the offer type: a larger size of the same product (the source's example is a 24-ounce coffee bag instead of the 12-ounce) or a cross-sell based on the purchased item ('Jane, would you like to add the matching silk pillowcase to your new sheet set?').
- For a skincare store, the source's example framing is: 'Before you go, complete your skincare routine with this moisturizer. Enjoy 20% off today.'
- Keep the offer relevant to the item just purchased so it reads as completing the purchase rather than as new selling.
- Test discount-tied versus no-discount variants of the same offer.
Condition: No conversion figures are attached to post-purchase upsells in the source; the recommendation is a stated best practice from Yotpo's guidance.
Condition: Confirm platform support and explicit customer acceptance before charging or changing an order. Report net incremental contribution after discounts, fulfillment and refunds.

[f6a8fc1ece5f868123f1e355] Target the First-to-Second Purchase Gap as the Hardest Retention Step
Applies when: Deciding where to invest retention/win-back effort — loyalty, post-purchase, and win-back flows — and setting expectations for which cohort to focus on.
- Recognize the source's framing: going from a first-time buyer to a second-time buyer is the hardest step; once a customer has bought 2–3 times, getting them to buy again is comparatively easy.
- Design the post-purchase flow (loyalty intro, review request, cross-sell) specifically to shorten that first-to-second gap.
- Use the win-back flow to catch first-time buyers who never returned within your typical buying cycle (see win-back card).
- In the loyalty introduction email, emphasize earning points and discounts on the next purchase to lower the barrier for a second order.
- Treat first-time buyer retention as the metric to watch, not just total repeat rate.
Condition: This is the presenter's framing of relative difficulty, not a measured benchmark — your category may differ.
Condition: Durability and consumable products may have structurally shorter repurchase cycles than the source's general claim.

[1784ea2727accf45dd31251e] Run 3-4 email campaigns per week to carry retention
Applies when: Planning weekly retention calendar and deciding how much to rely on automation versus broadcasts.
- Send 3-4 campaigns per week (the source treats two as the floor).
- Use these campaigns as your testing ground for angles that later get ported into flows.
- Keep the win-back flow simple because recipients are still receiving your regular campaigns.
- Expect most repeat purchases to come from campaigns — the source asserts around 99% of retention and repeat purchases, but treat this as the presenter's claim, not a measured figure for your list.
- Watch engagement and unsubscribes when scaling frequency; adjust if list health degrades.
Condition: The 99% claim is an unverified assertion in the source; do not plan forecasts around it.

[42e1ab9189e1ae54481f7067] Diagnose weak second-purchase conversion before blaming email copy
Applies when: Interpreting a poor repeat purchase rate and deciding whether the issue is execution (emails) or foundations (product, portfolio, acquisition, experience).
- Assume the 80/20 non-repeat pattern is often a foundations problem before blaming messaging. Review the retention hierarchy top-down.
- Check acquisition quality, since bargain-hunting and low-AOV acquisition channels predict lower repeat behaviour.
- Check the product portfolio for natural cross-sell, upsell or replenishment. Without a reason to return, no flow will fix the number.
- Confirm the customer journey is mapped into your account as new/returning/loyal paths; without that structure, you cannot even isolate the constraint.
- Look at whether the store is misreading signals: e.g., relying on attribution dashboards and returning-customer percentage that improve when acquisition gets worse.
Condition: The 80% figure comes from the source's framing that only around 20% of customers buy a second time from most brands; treat it as an observed pattern rather than a hard benchmark.
Condition: Not every brand is in the same category — repeat rates differ widely between CPG, fashion and one-off products.

[55f0042df14c6c6ba61d7ef8] Educate customers across the journey to drive repeat purchase
Applies when: When planning content, email or video assets against specific stage outcomes to reduce returns and increase repeat rate.
- Awareness: teach the problem and the desired outcome, not the spec. Beardbrand built 1,000+ YouTube grooming videos (1.6M+ subscribers) that fed its move from online-only to Target; Glossier built Into the Gloss community before product.
- Consideration: teach trade-offs and fit through quizzes, comparison pages, AR and UGC; tell customers when a product is not right for them to cut returns and earn trust.
- Delivery gap: teach first use and build anticipation with drip emails and SMS while the customer waits; boAt sends usage instructions plus a next-order discount.
- Onboarding: send a personalized day-by-day usage plan tied to the purchased item and outcome; measure activation rate and 60-day repeat rate.
- Retention: teach advanced use and adjacent needs via newsletters and replenishment tips to set up cross-sell.
- Measure content-attributed signups and assisted conversions; content with no link to the product problem is just cost.
Condition: Beardbrand and Glossier are illustrative examples, not controlled studies of content ROI.
Condition: Long-form content is personality- and resource-intensive; Dollar Shave Club-style viral content is hard to repeat.

[7ccc6c565f867390e76167f0] Build buyer, non-buyer and repeat-buyer segments for tailored messaging
Applies when: Planning campaigns and flows that treat new, repeat and never-purchased customers differently.
- All buyers: person can receive email marketing AND placed order at least once over all time.
- First-time buyers: clone the buyers segment and set placed order equals 1 over all time.
- 2x buyers: placed order equals 2 over all time; 3x+ (VIP candidates): placed order at least 3 over all time.
- Non-buyers: placed order 0 times over all time — this list-only, never-purchased group should get different campaigns and flows than repeat buyers because their mindset differs.
- Use these groups to size your customer base (how many buyers, first-timers, repeat buyers, never-bought) and to target appropriate offers.
Condition: Cloning and editing one base segment is faster than building each from scratch.
Condition: Thresholds (e.g. 3+ = VIP candidate) are starting points, not fixed definitions.

[c076b110d253f505c1dbae09] Use feature holdouts to measure net revenue, not proxy engagement
Applies when: Evaluating an email popup, product-recommendation module, onsite quiz, personalization engine, or similar feature that affects both engagement and the buying journey.
- Randomly reserve a control group that never sees the feature while the remaining eligible traffic receives it. The source illustrates 90% exposed and 10% held out for a popup, and a 5% feature holdout for recommendations.
- Track both groups through purchase and, where relevant, subsequent repeat purchase; do not stop reporting at an email or SMS signup.
- Measure revenue per visitor as the decision metric, supported by conversion rate, AOV, margin if available, and opt-in rate.
- Look for trade-offs. A popup can raise email capture while interrupting product discovery and lowering purchase conversion; a recommendation module can increase clicks without increasing total basket value.
- Segment only when sample size supports it, such as new versus returning visitors or mobile versus desktop, and ensure the primary decision is based on the predeclared overall metric.
- Keep the holdout in place long enough to capture delayed purchases and repeat behavior when the feature is intended to affect them.
Condition: The source provides example split ratios but no required sample size or duration.
Condition: A feature can affect future marketing eligibility, so short-term purchase measurement may miss some longer-term value or harm.

[d7082f8c3c813a3e82f869da] Welcome flow as the primary retention vehicle
Applies when: Designing post-purchase email/SMS, or trying to lift repeat purchase and LTV.
- Build a welcome flow that runs after the first purchase and is treated as the primary retention mechanism, not an afterthought receipt.
- Include a post-purchase survey in the flow to capture how the customer found you and why they bought.
- Split-test the discount depth in the flow — the source describes testing discount level rather than assuming the biggest offer wins.
- Use the flow to introduce the product line and set purchase expectations so first orders do not return.
- Measure the flow's effect on repeat rate, not just open rates.
- Verify the current capabilities of your email/SMS platform before building.
Condition: Deep welcome discounts train customers to wait for discounts; the source treats discount depth as something to test, echoing that tension.

[0005f05fcb3211e0bef1cd69] Measure Retention by Fundamentals, Not Email KPIs
Applies when: Diagnosing poor repeat purchase rates before investing in more email flows, upsells or cross-sells.
- First establish your baseline: check whether a meaningful portion of customers return on their own without marketing intervention. The source says you should; if you don't, extra marketing will not create it.
- Walk the retention drivers the source lists — product quality, product portfolio, repeatability, customer experience, competitive landscape, pricing and the broader economy — and treat them as the upstream causes.
- Use email and owned media to amplify those fundamentals: the source notes good brands use email to foster community, build loyalty and VIP programs, and run abandonment sequences.
- In flows, prioritize communicating things that affect the customer experience — the source's example is that complex or instruction-dependent products should be explained rather than immediately pushed toward an upsell or cross-sell.
- Treat Klaviyo (or any ESP) as a channel that can improve or worsen experience, but not as the fix for deep retention problems.
Condition: This is the presenters' strong opinion ('retention is not a flows problem, most of the time') and is framed against common agency pitches — it is a prioritization argument, not a claim that flows are unimportant.
Condition: The five-driver list is a conversational enumeration, not a formal framework.

[8dd8db3f346d5f0659b1299d] Distinguish reward-driven purchases from durable product preference
Applies when: Evaluating a discounted trial or loyalty incentive.
- State the incentive and its duration before customers join.
- Measure repeat purchases and product satisfaction after the disclosed reward period.
- Compare with a suitable baseline before attributing retention to brand preference.
Condition: Honor promised rewards; historical psychology findings do not establish ecommerce retention rates.

[b3058403e9f86ef7e5e7523b] Post-purchase as the retention engine
Applies when: Deciding how much post-purchase and replenishment effort to invest after the first order.
- Reframe the first purchase as the beginning of the relationship — a weak post-purchase experience loses repeat purchases, referrals, trust, and lifetime value.
- Prioritize the first 30 days: the source says most returning customers buy within 30 days of their initial order, so this is the window to improve first-to-second purchase rate.
- Use the flow to reduce returns by reinforcing purchase value, giving usage/care tips, and building excitement — buyer's remorse is a major return driver and returns cut into margin.
- Push replenishment appropriately within the post-purchase sequence: subscriptions or loyalty programs for replenishable products, and cross-sell/recommendations for everything else.
- Multi-channel touchpoints (email + SMS + social) are described as ways to increase repurchase rate — the more places you hold the customer, the more often you can reach them.
Condition: The statistics cited (9x, 67%, 95%, 30-day window) are attributed to 'research' by the source without citations and are not benchmarks you should plan against.
Condition: Return-rate and repeat-purchase effects will vary by category and AOV; the source presents them as typical, not universal.

[e13b48c6a15a1a2a3b47a509] Segment Post-Purchase Flows by First-Time, Repeat and VIP Buyers
Applies when: Restructuring lifecycle email and on-site experience so loyal customers do not receive the same treatment as first-time shoppers.
- Segment your base into first-time buyers, repeat buyers and VIPs.
- For first-time buyers, focus the flow on education and brand story.
- For repeat buyers, focus on cross-selling into adjacent categories.
- For VIPs, focus on early access, exclusive experiences and recognition.
- Consider adding non-discount rewards — early access, exclusive content or experiential benefits — to differentiate from points-only competitors.
- Apply the same logic on-site: Princess Polly identified that multi-purchase customers received the identical on-site experience as one-time buyers and used personalization to make loyal customers feel valued.
- For lapsed customers, send valuable content instead of generic discounts: Matas, the Danish beauty retailer, ran a personalized re-engagement sequence that achieved a 29-point retention lift within 30 days while driving 20% more orders.
Condition: The Matas and Princess Polly results are single-brand examples; the source does not specify the exact segmentation criteria or cadence beyond first-time/repeat/VIP.

[6dcc8b256a6bc4e76c738d23] Time replenishment and second-purchase nudges to demand
Applies when: When setting up email/SMS flows for consumables or any store where the first-to-second purchase is the key retention gap.
- For consumables, nudge at roughly 75% of the customer's usage cycle rather than on a fixed calendar.
- Cap replenishment messages at about 2 per cycle to avoid reading as spam.
- Use the Chewy Autoship model in copy: 'running low? save 10%' frames the message as usefulness, not promotion.
- For non-consumables, send a second-purchase nudge about 10 days after the first order arrives with a modest 10-15% incentive focused on relevant discovery; expect 25-30% first-to-second conversion when done well.
- Give subscriptions real flexibility (change cadence, skip, pause) because rigid subscriptions drive cancellations and chargebacks.
- Track reorder rate, 90-day repeat rate and subscription adoption.
Condition: The 8-15% vs 1-3% conversion figures are industry/vendor benchmarks, not controlled studies.
Condition: Wrong timing or too many messages reads as nagging and can increase unsubscribes.
